lessons.title: Represent Rational Numbers on the Coordinate Plane
lessons.objective: I can plot and identify points on the coordinate plane using ordered pairs.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words coordinate plane, ordered pair, origin, and quadrant.

concept.heading: How do you plot a point on the coordinate plane?
concept.intro: An ordered pair (x, y) is two numbers that tell you exactly where a point goes. The first number moves you right or left. The second number moves you up or down.
concept.keyIdea: Coordinate Plane: Plotting Points. Formula: Ordered Pair: (x, y) = (Horizontal, Vertical). 1. Always start at the Origin (0, 0). 2. x-coordinate: Move right for positive (+), left for negative (-). 3. y-coordinate: Move up for positive (+), down for negative (-)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot the point (5, 4). The 5 is the x-coordinate, and the 4 is the y-coordinate.
I start at the origin, which is (0, 0).
First I move 5 units to the right along the x-axis.
Then I move 4 units up. I place my dot. That is the point (5, 4).
linesEs: Voy a marcar el punto (5, 4). El 5 es la coordenada x, y el 4 es la coordenada y.
Empiezo en el origen, que es (0, 0).
Primero me muevo 5 unidades a la derecha por el eje x.
Luego me muevo 4 unidades hacia arriba. Coloco mi punto. Ese es el punto (5, 4).

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's plot (2, 1). Where do we start? At the origin (0, 0).
How far do we move right? The first number is 2, so we move 2 right.
How far do we move up? The second number is 1, so we move 1 up and place the dot.
linesEs: Ahora marquemos (2, 1). ¿Dónde empezamos? En el origen (0, 0).
¿Cuánto nos movemos a la derecha? El primer número es 2, así que nos movemos 2 a la derecha.
¿Cuánto nos movemos hacia arriba? El segundo número es 1, así que subimos 1 y colocamos el punto.

vocabulary.definition: Plot a point by moving horizontally to its x-coordinate and vertically to its y-coordinate.
vocabulary.example: For (3, −2), move right 3 and down 2.

vocabulary.definition: A grid with a line going across and a line going up to plot points.
vocabulary.example: A grid with a horizontal line (x-axis) crossing a vertical line (y-axis), making four sections

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that tell where a point is on a grid.
vocabulary.example: (3, 5) means move right 3 from the origin, then up 5

vocabulary.definition: The point (0, 0) where the two grid lines cross.
vocabulary.example: The starting point at the center where both axes cross — (0, 0)

vocabulary.definition: One of the four parts of a coordinate grid, numbered I to IV.
vocabulary.example: I (+,+) top-right, II (-,+) top-left, III (-,-) bottom-left, IV (+,-) bottom-right

vocabulary.definition: A flipped, mirror image across a line.
vocabulary.example: (3, 2) reflected over the x-axis becomes (3, -2) — same x, opposite y

vocabulary.definition: Whole numbers and their opposites, like -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.
The first number in an ordered pair; how far right or left.
vocabulary.example: In (−3, 4), the x-coordinate is −3.

vocabulary.definition: The horizontal number line through the origin.
vocabulary.example: Runs left and right.

vocabulary.definition: The vertical number line through the origin.
vocabulary.example: Runs up and down.

lessons.title: Determine Distance on the Coordinate Plane
lessons.objective: I can find the distance between two points on the coordinate plane using absolute value.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words distance, absolute value, horizontal distance, and vertical distance.

concept.heading: How do you find distance on the coordinate plane?
concept.intro: Distance is how far apart two points are, and it is never negative. When two points share a row or a column, you can find the distance using their coordinates.
concept.keyIdea: Distance on the Coordinate Plane. Formula: Distance = |x1 − x2| (horizontal) or |y1 − y2| (vertical). 1. Same quadrant / Same sign: Subtract absolute values of differing coordinates. 2. Different quadrants / Opposite signs: Add absolute values of differing coordinates. 3. Distance is never negative; it is zero when both points coincide

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I will find the distance from (-3, 2) to (4, 2). Both have y = 2, so they sit on the same horizontal line.
The points are on opposite sides of zero, so I add the absolute values.
I add: 3 + 4 = 7. The distance between them is 7 units.
linesEs: Voy a hallar la distancia de (-3, 2) a (4, 2). Los dos tienen y = 2, así que están en la misma línea horizontal.
Los puntos están en lados opuestos del cero, así que sumo los valores absolutos.
Sumo: 3 + 4 = 7. La distancia entre ellos es de 7 unidades.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now let's find the distance from (2, 3) to (2, 8). What do these points share? The same x = 2, so it is a vertical line.
These points are on the SAME side of zero (both positive), so do we add or subtract? We subtract.
The distance is |8 - 3| = 5 units. When points sit on the same side of zero, subtract to find the distance.
linesEs: Ahora hallemos la distancia de (2, 3) a (2, 8). ¿Qué comparten estos puntos? La misma x = 2, así que es una línea vertical.
Estos puntos están del mismo lado del cero (los dos positivos), entonces ¿sumamos o restamos? Restamos.
La distancia es |8 - 3| = 5 unidades. Cuando los puntos están del mismo lado del cero, resta para hallar la distancia.

vocabulary.definition: The nonnegative distance between points, found from the absolute difference of coordinates on a horizontal or vertical line.
How far apart two points are. It is never negative.
vocabulary.example: The distance from -3 to 4 on a number line is |-3| + |4| = 3 + 4 = 7 units

vocabulary.definition: How far a number is from zero. It is never negative.
vocabulary.example: |-3| = 3 and |4| = 4; to find distance: |4 - (-3)| = 7

vocabulary.definition: How far apart two points are going left or right.
vocabulary.example: From (-2, 3) to (5, 3): count from -2 to 5 = 7 units across

vocabulary.definition: How far apart two points are going up or down.
vocabulary.example: From (4, -1) to (4, 6): count from -1 to 6 = 7 units up

vocabulary.definition: A grid with a line going across and a line going up to plot points.
vocabulary.example: Two number lines crossing at (0, 0), creating four quadrants

vocabulary.definition: Whole numbers and their opposites, like -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.
One of the four regions of the coordinate plane, numbered I to IV.
vocabulary.example: Points in the same quadrant have the same signs.

create: Design a delivery route with three axis-aligned segments. List every endpoint and segment distance, then calculate and justify the total route length.

support.prompt: Which ordered pair names a point 3 units right and 7 units up from the origin?
support.explanation: The first coordinate is horizontal (right 3), the second is vertical (up 7). So (3, 7).
feedback: The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
hints: Re-read the moves: 3 units right, then 7 units up. Which move comes first in an ordered pair?
An ordered pair is (x, y): x is the right/left distance, y is the up/down distance. Match each move to its slot.
Start at the origin and go right 3 — that 3 is the x, the first number. Now decide where the 'up 7' goes.

support.prompt: What are the coordinates of the origin?
support.explanation: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis cross, at (0, 0).
feedback: Both coordinates at the origin are 0 — not mixed with 1.
The origin is where both axes cross, where both values are zero.
The origin is where the two axes cross each other. At that crossing point, how far along is each axis? That tells you both coordinates.
hints: The origin is the exact spot where the x-axis and y-axis cross. Picture that crossing point.
Ask: how far right have you moved at the origin? How far up? Those two distances are the coordinates.
At the crossing point you haven't moved right at all, so x = 0. Now figure out the y-value the same way.

support.prompt: A point is at (6, 2). What does the 6 tell you?
support.explanation: The first number (x-coordinate) tells you horizontal movement. 6 means go right 6 units from the origin.
feedback: The first number controls horizontal movement—check which number moves you up.
With a positive first number, you move right—not left.
Not quite. The first number (x-coordinate) tells you horizontal movement.
hints: In (6, 2), the 6 is the FIRST number. First and second positions have different jobs.
First number = x = horizontal (right/left). Second number = y = vertical (up/down). Positive means right or up.
The 6 sits in the x spot and it's positive, so it describes a horizontal move. Which direction is positive x?

steps: Clue: Plot the point (5, 2).
Start: Start at the origin (0, 0). Good.
Move up: Move 5 units UP along the y-axis.
Move right: Move 2 units to the right. Place the dot at (2, 5).
support.explanation: The student moved UP first. The FIRST number (5) is the x-coordinate, so move 5 units RIGHT; then the SECOND number (2) is the y-coordinate, so move 2 units UP. The point is (5, 2), not (2, 5).
hints: Which direction does the first number in (x, y) tell you to move — right or up?
The first number is always the horizontal (right) move. Here that is 5 right, then 2 up.

support.prompt: What is the distance between (-4, 3) and (2, 3)?
support.explanation: Both points have y = 3, so this is a horizontal distance. |2 - (-4)| = |2 + 4| = 6 units.
feedback: 2 is the difference of the sizes 4 and 2, but the points sit on OPPOSITE sides of zero. Count the units from -4 to 0, then from 0 to 2, and combine them.
It looks like you counted from -4 only as far as 0 and stopped there. The segment keeps going past the origin to x = 2, so there are more units to add on.
This is the distance you would get if the second point were at x = 4 instead of x = 2. Find 2 on the x-axis and count only that far.
hints: Both points have y = 3, so they sit on the same horizontal line — only the x-values differ.
Find the gap between x = -4 and x = 2. The path crosses zero, so add the two distances |-4| and |2|.
Count from -4 to 0 (that's 4 units), then from 0 to 2. Add the two parts together.

support.prompt: What is the distance between (5, -2) and (5, 4)?
support.explanation: Both points have x = 5, so this is a vertical distance. |4 - (-2)| = |4 + 2| = 6 units.
feedback: 2 only counts part of the trip. The segment runs from y = -2 all the way up to y = 4 — the units below zero and above zero both count.
You counted the part above the x-axis, from 0 up to 4, but the segment starts below the axis at -2. Add the units under zero too.
It looks like you combined the x-coordinates (5 and 5) instead of the y-coordinates. The x-values match here, which is the clue that the segment is vertical — the y-values are what change.
hints: Both points share x = 5 — the segment is VERTICAL, so compare the y-values -2 and 4.
The path crosses zero: split it into a below-zero part and an above-zero part using absolute values.
From y = -2 up to 0 is 2 units; from 0 up to 4 is 4 more. Add the parts.

support.prompt: A rectangle has vertices at (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4), (1, 4). What is its perimeter?
feedback: The rectangle has four sides, and this only accounts for the two horizontal ones. After doubling the width, add the two vertical sides as well.
Not quite. Width = 5 - 1 = ___.
You used the coordinates 5 and 5 as if they were the side lengths. A coordinate tells you where a corner sits, not how long a side is — subtract the two x-values and the two y-values first.
hints: Perimeter is the distance all the way around — you need the width AND the height first.
Width: subtract the x-values 5 and 1. Height: subtract the y-values 4 and 1. Then add all four sides.
Find 5 − 1 for the width and 4 − 1 for the height. Now double each and add — that covers all four sides.

steps: Problem: Find the distance between (2, 1) and (2, 6).
Student thinking: Both share x = 2, so add the absolute values: |1| + |6| = 1 + 6 = 7.
Student answer: The distance is 7 units.
support.explanation: Both points are on the same side of zero (1 and 6 are both positive), so you SUBTRACT instead of adding. The distance is |6 - 1| = 5 units. The student should only add the absolute values when the points are on opposite sides of zero. The correct distance is 5 units, not 7.
hints: Are 1 and 6 on the same side of zero or opposite sides?
When both coordinates are on the same side of zero, subtract: |6 - 1| = ___.

support.prompt: Predict the street-route distance for these settings. Give the answer in units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: Horizontal 5 + vertical 0 = 5. A (-3, 4), B (2, 4). The two points share an axis-aligned street.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: What is the horizontal distance from (−3, 4) to (2, 4)?
support.explanation: The y-coordinates match, so distance = |2 − (−3)| = 5 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: What is the vertical distance from (2, −5) to (2, 3)?
support.explanation: The x-coordinates match, so distance = |3 − (−5)| = 8 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

steps: Clue: Plot the point (4, 0).
Move right: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis. Good.
Move up: Move 4 units up, because the pair has a 4 in it.
Plot the point: Place the dot at (4, 4).
core.explanation: The y-coordinate is 0, not 4. After moving 4 right, the up move is 0 units, so the point stays on the x-axis at (4, 0). The student reused the x-value instead of reading the second number (0).
hints: What is the SECOND number in (4, 0), and how far up does it tell you to move?
A y-coordinate of 0 means do not move up at all — the point sits right on the x-axis at (4, 0).

core.prompt: Two points are at (-3, -7) and (-3, 5). What is the distance between them?
feedback: Not quite. Distance = |5 - (-7)| = |5 + 7| = ___.
You counted the part below the x-axis, from -7 up to 0, and stopped. The second point is at y = 5, which is above the axis, so there is more to count.
It looks like you combined -3 with 5 — that mixes an x-coordinate with a y-coordinate. Both points share x = -3, so the numbers that change are the y-values.
hints: Both points share x = -3, so this is a vertical distance between y = -7 and y = 5.
The y-values have opposite signs, so add their absolute values instead of just subtracting the digits.
Count from -7 up to 0 (that's 7 units), then from 0 up to 5. Add the two counts.

core.prompt: What is the distance between (2, 3) and (2, 8)?
core.explanation: The x-coordinates match, so distance = |8 - 3| = 5 units.
feedback: This is the halfway point between 3 and 8, not the gap between them. Subtract the two y-coordinates instead of averaging them.
It looks like you counted the grid lines 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 instead of the hops between them. Distance counts the spaces, so the starting line does not get counted.
Not quite. The x-coordinates match, so distance = |8 - 3| = ___.
hints: The x's match (both 2), so the distance is just the gap between y = 3 and y = 8.
Both y-values are on the same side of zero here — subtract the smaller y from the larger y.
Set up 8 − 3 and work it out. That count of units is your distance.

core.prompt: What is the distance between (-4, 1) and (3, 1)?
core.explanation: The y-coordinates match, so distance = |3 - (-4)| = 7 units.
feedback: A distance can never be negative, because it just counts units. If your subtraction comes out negative, take the absolute value of it.
Not quite. The y-coordinates match, so distance = |3 - (-4)| = ___.
It looks like you multiplied 4 and 3. When a segment crosses zero, the two pieces get added together, not multiplied — count the hops on each side of the origin.
hints: The y's match (both 1), so it's a horizontal gap between x = -4 and x = 3.
The x-values have opposite signs: add the distances |-4| and |3| instead of subtracting 4 − 3.
Count -4 to 0 (4 units), then 0 to 3 (3 units). Combine the parts — a distance is never negative.

steps: Problem: Find the distance between (-5, 2) and (3, 2).
Student thinking: Both share y = 2, so subtract the x-values: 5 - 3 = 2.
Student answer: The distance is 2 units.
core.explanation: The student dropped the negative sign and used 5 instead of -5. The point is at x = -5, so the two points sit on opposite sides of zero. Add the absolute values: |-5| + |3| = 5 + 3 = 8 units. (You can also write |3 - (-5)| = |3 + 5| = 8.) The correct distance is 8 units, not 2.
hints: The first x-coordinate is -5, not 5. Did the student keep the negative sign?
The points are on opposite sides of zero, so add: |-5| + |3| = ___.

core.prompt: Predict the street-route distance for these settings. Give the answer in units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: Horizontal 4 + vertical 0 = 4. A (-2, 4), B (2, 4). The two points share an axis-aligned street.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: What is the horizontal distance from (−3, 4) to (2, 4)?
core.explanation: The y-coordinates match, so distance = |2 − (−3)| = 5 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: What is the vertical distance from (2, −5) to (2, 3)?
core.explanation: The x-coordinates match, so distance = |3 − (−5)| = 8 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

steps: Ordered pair: (7, 3)
Move along the x-axis: Start at the origin (0, 0) and count 7 units to the right.
Move along the y-axis: Count up from the x-axis: 1, 2, 3, 4 — stop on 4.
Plot the point: Place the dot at (7, 4).
stretch.explanation: The x-axis itself is 0, not 1. Counting up correctly: 1, 2, 3 — the third count lands on y = 3, so the point is (7, 3), not (7, 4). The student started counting one gridline too high by treating the x-axis as unit 1 instead of unit 0.
hints: When you count up from the x-axis, is the x-axis itself unit 0 or unit 1?
The x-axis is 0. The first line above it is 1, the second is 2, the third is 3. So 3 units up lands on y = 3, not y = 4.

stretch.prompt: A student says that (3, 5) and (5, 3) are the same point because they use the same numbers. Is the student correct? Explain why or why not, and describe where each point is located on the coordinate plane.
stretch.frame: The student is ___ because (3, 5) means ___ while (5, 3) means ___. The ORDER matters because ___.
stretch.explanation: The student is not correct. In (3, 5) the 3 is the x-coordinate, so you move right 3 and up 5, landing high and toward the left. In (5, 3) the 5 is the x-coordinate, so you move right 5 and up 3, landing lower and farther right. Same digits, different jobs — the order inside an ordered pair decides which direction each number controls.
hints: Both pairs use 3 and 5, but look at which number sits in the x (first) spot in each pair.
Describe each point's moves separately: (3, 5) = right ?, up ?; (5, 3) = right ?, up ?. Compare the two paths.
First step: for (3, 5), go right 3 and up 5. Now do (5, 3)'s moves and check whether you land on the same dot.

stretch.prompt: A rectangle has corners (1, 2), (1, 5), (5, 5), and (5, 2). What is its perimeter?
stretch.explanation: Width = |5 - 1| = 4, height = |5 - 2| = 3, so perimeter = 2(4 + 3) = 14 units. (Area would be 12 sq units, so perimeter and area are different here.)
feedback: Not quite. Width = |5 - 1| = 4, height = |5 - 2| = 3, so perimeter = 2(4 + 3) = ___.
It looks like you doubled the coordinate 5 rather than an actual side length. Subtract to get the width and the height first, then go around all four sides.
You found 4 × 3, which is the space inside the rectangle. Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside, so add the four side lengths instead.
hints: It's a rectangle: the two x-values (1 and 5) and two y-values (2 and 5) build the sides.
Width = |5 − 1| and height = |5 − 2|. The perimeter adds ALL four sides — not just one width and one height.
Find 5 − 1 and 5 − 2 first. Then double each result and add them together.

stretch.prompt: How far apart are the points (-2, 5) and (-2, -3)?
stretch.explanation: The x-coordinates match, so distance = |5 - (-3)| = 8 units.
feedback: Distance is never negative. Take the absolute value of the difference between the y-coordinates.
Not quite. The x-coordinates match, so distance = |5 - (-3)| = ___.
It looks like you multiplied 5 and 3. The two pieces of a segment that crosses the x-axis get added, so count the units above zero and the units below zero and combine them.
hints: The x's match (both -2), so measure the vertical gap between y = 5 and y = -3.
Opposite signs on the y-values: the distance is |5| plus |-3|, the two distances from zero combined.
Count from 5 down to 0, then from 0 down to −3. Add the two counts. These are distinct points, so their distance is greater than zero.

steps: Problem: Find the distance between (-3, 4) and (5, 4)
Student thinking: Subtract: 5 - 3 = 2
Student answer: The distance is 2 units
stretch.explanation: The student subtracted 5 - 3, but the first x-coordinate is -3, not 3. The correct calculation is |5 - (-3)| = |5 + 3| = 8 units. When points span opposite sides of an axis, you must add the absolute values: |-3| + |5| = 3 + 5 = 8.
hints: The student dropped the negative sign on -3. What is the actual difference between -3 and 5?
Try counting on the number line from -3 to 5. How many units is that?

stretch.prompt: A rectangle has vertices at (-4, -2), (3, -2), (3, 5), and (-4, 5). Find the length, width, perimeter, and area of the rectangle. Show your work using absolute value.
stretch.frame: The width is |___ - (___)| = ___ units. The height is |___ - (___)| = ___ units. The perimeter is 2(___ + ___) = ___ units. The area is ___ × ___ = ___ square units.
stretch.explanation: The width comes from the two x-values, |3 - (-4)| = 7, and the height comes from the two y-values, |5 - (-2)| = 7, so this rectangle is actually a square. That gives a perimeter of 2(7 + 7) = 28 units and an area of 7 × 7 = 49 square units.
hints: Width uses the two x-values (-4 and 3); height uses the two y-values (-2 and 5). Each pair has opposite signs.
Use absolute value: width = |3 − (-4)| and height = |5 − (-2)|. Then perimeter = 2(w + h) and area = w × h.
Start with the width: |3 − (-4)| means 3 + 4. Work that out, then set up the height the same way.

stretch.prompt: Predict the street-route distance for these settings. Give the answer in units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
stretch.explanation: Horizontal 3 + vertical 0 = 3. A (-1, 4), B (2, 4). The two points share an axis-aligned street.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

stretch.explanation: The y-coordinates match, so distance = |2 − (−3)| = 5 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.explanation: The x-coordinates match, so distance = |3 − (−5)| = 8 units.
